utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It was announced that the Prosecution wanted to raise a preliminary issue -- Defence wanted to raise a preliminary issue. I apologise. You are equal for me, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. I just actually spoke with my learned friends from the opposite side, and we agreed, I think, that if there is a large document envisaged to be used during the cross-examination, that they would mark the page so we do not have to print, like, 500 pages document, and we are actually both willing to save some trees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. And the trees will appreciate it as well, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that's all we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that sounds very reasonable and very practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I agree, it is reasonable, and I have already sent an instruction to the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's great. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've advised the Defence in advance that after reviewing the transcript from yesterday, there's going to be no further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Radan. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The Chamber was informed by the Prosecution that they have no further questions for you in cross-examination. However, Judge Moloto has a further question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes at page 35, line 23, of the transcript, you answered the question about the population of your area at the time. You said: "Well, earlier we were not divided and there were no divisions by where people lived, but we are talking about a majority. A majority of Serbian population lived there. Most of the people were Serbs, but previously nobody paid attention to that." Do you remember that piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you are -- in your statement, you stated that: According to the population census of 1991, Novo Sarajevo municipality had a total of 95.089 inhabitants, of whom 35 per cent were Muslim, 35 per cent Serbs, and 9 per cent Croats, 15 per cent Yugoslavs, and 4 per cent others. Surely according to this statement, Serbs were not in the majority. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the entire municipality, according to the census, they were not a majority, but there were quite a few of those who were not one or the other or the third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the point. The point is -- the Serbs were not in the majority.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the correct position, not what you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I spoke about the territory that was under the control after the beginning of the war, under our control; that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. We were talking about Novo Sarajevo municipality. But, anyway, thank you so much. I just wanted to get that point clear. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one question for you as well. In paragraph 21 of your statement, you say: "At the beginning of the war, most of the victims were killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side," and then you explained that every single day, from early morning until dusk, snipers fired from Debelo Brdo, the Executive Council building, the, as you corrected it, the Bristol Hotel, and so on. If you are talking about the beginning of the war, what period of time do you have exactly in mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning from the war is from the 4th of the April, 1992. That is to say, in that period all the way up until the end of the war, there was sniper fire coming from those positions that I mentioned. It was aimed at the territory of Grbavica and Vrace. That is to say, the urban areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since you used the language "at the beginning of the war," I understood that this may have changed during the war. Or were, during the whole of the war, most of the victims killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side? And if not, up until what moment were most victims killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side? I'm trying to get a better idea of the time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat activities took place practically every day. Whereas sniper activity was sporadic, and that was a response to certain individual situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- you're telling apparently things you want to tell me but you seem not to be very inclined to answer my questions. You said: "At the beginning of the war, most of the victims were killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side." Now let me first try to understand that. Do you mean that more victims were killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side than victims were killed by sniper fire from the Serb side? Or are you comparing victims of sniper fire, victims of Muslim sniping fire, against all victims of war, among the Muslims apparently killed by Serb fire? What exactly are you telling us here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to give you an accurate answer, I would need to elaborate at length. It could not have been systematised in terms of months, let alone days. So that is to say that all of this was caused by the situation itself on the ground. That is to say, it was impossible to say when there was more of what and so on and so forth. Special records were kept by those who were keeping records of fatalities, the wounded and so on. All of this information was not accessible to me every day. These records were kept by the civilian police, the hospitals, the funeral parlours, and so on, so they kept these records. However, in order for me to give you a complete answer that I wish, I'm not in a position to give it now. It could not have been systematised in the following way. For example, to say during the first month, this was the number of sniper victims from the sniper fire coming from the Muslim side. We don't even have figures about the other side, and the fighting was intensified as the situation developed. And from the beginning of May, from Dobrovoljacka onwards, fighting was intensified on all sides. That is to say, we were Grbavica. Grbavica was surrounded on three sides; that is to say, from Debelo Brdo -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. First of all, I'm re-reading again now the first line. In order to understand what it means. It says: "At the beginning of the war, most of the victims were killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side." Now, that can be understood in two different ways. The one is most of the victims of snipers were killed by Muslim snipers. Or, and that's another way of understanding this sentence, at the beginning of the war, most of the victims, overall victims, were killed by sniper fire from the Muslim side. So there the emphasise on whether it was sniper fire or any other fire, that's a way of understanding it. Whereas the first way of understanding this language would be more people killed by sniper fire by the Muslims than people were killed by sniper fire from the Serbs. Now, which of the two are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we focus on this statement, "in the beginning of the war," then, if we exclude the incident in Dobrovoljacka, the beginning of the war, if we exclude that, then we could say that there were more victims from sniper fire in the beginning of the war. That is to say, from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still unclear. Do you intend to say more people were killed by sniper fire than by shelling, by, whatever, other cause of death. Is that what you want to say? Or do you want to say there were more victims by sniper fire fired by Muslims than there were victims from sniper fire fired by Serbs? Which of the two is -- what do you tell us in this sentence? What are you comparing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a comparison as to how many casualties there were on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "most of the victims were killed by," that is already a comparison. That is more yes than no. Now, more yes what than --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is a comparison only on our side. That is the information we had available. How many victims there were, how many people were killed in combat, and how many were killed by sniper fire. So this was just on our side. It was impossible to carry out any kind of comparing with the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That clarifies a rather unclear sentence. So what you're telling us is that more people died from sniper fire than from combat or shelling or whatever other violence of war. It was sniper fire that caused most victims. And you can't compare that with what happened on the other side, whether there were more victims of sniper fire than shelling or more victims from shelling, or how many at all, you wouldn't know. That clarifies the matter considerably for me. Please proceed. Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Follow-up question to this issue. You just said -- a minute ago you told us that you base your information on the reports which were filed, the -- the records of your municipality from the hospitals, and so on. Is that the -- the source of information, or do you base it on your own observation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the basis of relevant records. My observations cannot cover the entire territory. So all of this was summed up from one period to another. It was either on a weekly basis or reports submitted to the Assembly, so these were just -- this was just relevant information that was collected from the police, from funeral parlours and so on. So only from these relevant sources, not based on my observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And these reports and written information, was that related only to Novo Sarajevo, to your municipality, or did you receive information also from other parts of the entire region?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was summed up at the level of the entire republic. I just had information in the territory of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you say "the entire republic," do you refer to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question. If you're talking about medical records and I'll be transparent, I've seen a few in my life, especially over the last ten years but also in this case. Often medical records say: Killed by a bullet. Vulnus sclopetarium or something like that. It comes immediately in Latin to my mind. How can you say that that is then someone killed by a sniper? I mean, what's the -- how could you draw any such conclusions on the basis of such medical records?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect for your assertion, I was never in a position to see that kind of very succinct report just saying: Killed by a bullet. Usually there's a description when and where this happened, whether somebody was just a passer-by was killed by sniper or whether somebody was killed in combat and so on. But not just killed by a bullet. I was not in a position to see a report like that. This was done by serious people who knew why they were doing this, and they realised that these records were being collected that would be relevant for the families involved and also later for those dealing with war victims and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was mainly referring to the strict medical reports. That is, what the doctor says when a body is brought in, into the hospital. But even if you have a broader report, is it -- I've heard often that people may have been killed by a stray bullet or by -- or that there was a military target nearby. How can you be so sure on the basis of those reports that the fire was sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go into that. I was not the one who would say whether the report was right or not. So those who wrote reports took an oath, as persons in the field of medicine, so they should write up everything they know. A stray bullet can also be identified as a bullet coming from a sniper or in combat. I just had an opportunity to see things stated that had actually happened and what the cause of death was, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say it depends in every individual case on the circumstances whether or not you can determine whether it was a bullet fired by a sniper or whether it was a bullet fired by any other combatant or person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now one additional question to that. How can a medical doctor in his report establish the ethnicity of the sniper?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't only medical doctors who were on this commission that kept the records. The doctor would not be the one who would assess the bullet and so on and so forth. This is being handed over to those who are professionals, who can establish the calibre of the ammunition involved, and at that time people knew who had what kind of ammunition, so this was the source on the basis of which it could be established with approximate accuracy whose bullet this was and where it had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At that point in time, at the beginning of the war, was it possible to distinguish by the ammunition from which side, from the Serb side or the Muslim side, the bullet was fired? Did they really have different ammunition at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not fully. Not 100 per cent. But it was known where these positions were from which fire had been coming. Professionals could establish this approximately, what the origin of the ammunition was and where it might have come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I will have to go through some documents the Prosecution used yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're not going to take very long today. You'll be free to go soon. I'm just going to ask you briefly about what the Judges had asked you about. Did you go into details of investigations or did you just take what other services had already established without any additional verification?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully trusted those who compiled those reports. I'm not the one who appointed them. Somebody else was in charge of that and what was taken into account was that these should be professional people and that they should work with full responsibility. So I fully trusted their reports without the right or obligation to double-check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask that we be shown in e-court P6524, a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to take it in the same order as the Prosecution did yesterday. Of course, the documents that I will be using, that is. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you able to read it without your glasses?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my sight is preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the 5th of June, 1992. It's a report on the activities. And, under item 3, it says accommodation of the population and refugees are mentioned. All refugees from the occupied territory and people who were left homeless, accommodation was provided for them. Who are these refugees? On the 5th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were mostly refugees who managed, who managed to cross into our territory from the territory that was under the control of the so-called Bosnia and Herzegovina Army. Armija. So people from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of those people who are referred to as refugees in this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they were Serbs. Serbs who were fleeing to our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I look at the next page, please, where we're going to focus on paragraph (f).

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This paragraph describes a shop under the control of the Crisis Staff where people can buy goods at prices set by the Executive Board. Could anybody buy goods in this shop, regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discriminate or divide people along ethnic lines. We didn't do that anywhere, and we did not do that here either. Nobody asked any questions of people who came to buy goods. The shop was under the control of the Crisis Staff and the Executive Board because, at that time, we did not have any company that could engage in such trade. So there was no division. We didn't discriminate among people in this shop or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page, please, where we will look at paragraph 6 -- item 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The paragraph says that frequently -- citizens of all nationalities assemble frequently, especially in Grbavica and our public attitude is very correct. We appoint a head of every building. Did you know how often were these meeting held? If you know, if you don't --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These meetings were not scheduled at certain times. They would just be held as needed, and the main goal was not to alarm the population, to calm the population. And if you permit me, I'm also going to say that at the beginning or shortly before the war broke out, we had barbecue barricades in response to the other barricades. And we called our citizens of other ethnic groups to socialise so that we can break down this fear, these stereotypes, and this was something filmed by different TV stations, federal ones, our TV stations, and it was broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. In the same paragraph, and there's a sentence that the Prosecution put a question to you about, and said: "Secretly the police applied the usual procedure towards people who were engaged in military activities against us." First, let me ask you this: Did you take part in any way in the police procedures relating to people engaged in military activities evidently here against us, meaning against the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never took part in any activities like that, but we had the military police, the civilian police force. We had a special commission that looked into specific incidents. These -- this data was summarised for the purposes of defence and also in order to calm down the situation in the field, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then in the next sentence you say -- actually, the document states: "We informed the Muslims that they would be safe if they were militarily neutral towards us, and so far the situation has been good." Could you please tell us how you informed the Muslims that they would be safe? Did you send them a message?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims could feel that they were safe because they were not separate in any way from Serbs and Croats. There was no discrimination. They were equal in relation to pensions, humanitarian aid, medical services, the central kitchens where milk was distributed every day to all citizens who needed the milk. They could not feel in any way that they were being discriminated against in relation to Serbs or anyone else. Thus, this was our way of showing that all citizens were the same to us and that the authorities that I was a part of were behaving in a legal manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next sentence towards the end of the document says: "We visited the nunnery in Gornji Kovacici." These nuns, what ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were Catholic nuns. They had everything they needed. Local Serbs, their neighbours, took care of them. At one time, because they were shelling on the other side, they said that they wanted to pull back from that place, but I personally went and asked them that, if they wanted to, we could relocate them but that they should remain on our territory. That time they did stay, but then later they didn't feel safe anymore and so they moved to a different location. And with the co-operation of Colonel Zarkovic, they crossed to the other side and went to Kiseljak. This is what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it does appear your question was not answered. You asked about ethnicity; you were told about the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Balkans it is very often mixed, but I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radan, could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Croats. Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout the war, in the Novo Sarajevo municipality, in Grbavica, that was under Serb control, did any Muslims remain there throughout the entire war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to our records, there was about 1.350 to 1.450 or 1.500 who -- Muslims who were there at the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just briefly look at the next page in the same document. We're going to look at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here on this page - we don't need to read everything - but there was a municipality by the president of the Presidency of Republika Srpska to form War Presidencies. And then the document states that there was no need for that in the Novo Sarajevo municipality area. But a Municipal Assembly is suggested, in turn, that it should be established. The Novo Sarajevo Municipal Assembly existed before the war also; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So why was there a need for it to be formed again?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the division and polarisation, all the main municipal infrastructure in Novo Sarajevo was on the other side, in the federal part. All the institutions, the Municipal Assembly were all on that side. And the things that we had at our disposal, we had about 25 councilmen who remained in that area, so there was an initiative to form the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, Serb Novo Sarajevo, again, and we assembled all the councilmen who were in our territory, and we held a founding Assembly session, and that, in turn, could elect all the other structures of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at P352 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we leave this document. A few minutes ago you told us that you informed the Muslims in your area that everything is -- is okay and there was no discrimination and everybody was prepared to stay. Now you're saying the Municipal Assembly had to be constituted consisting of the Serb municipal -- Municipal Assembly because of all the divisions. Are you able to distinguish exactly at what stage this took place, if -- I don't see why there should be a -- a Serb-only Municipal Assembly if relations were as good as you explained them. Can you just clarify that little apparent inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it was not the desire of the Serb population to undergo divisions. It was not at our initiative. The divisions - I don't want to go back to dates now and when the war broke out - but the division and the name of the Novo Sarajevo Serb municipality is a legal heritage. In order for us to be legal, to have legal status, we had to form our own municipality. This was a conclusion of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So that is the basis on which we formed it. The municipality councilmen were all Serbs because no Muslim or Croat councilmen happened to be on our territory. Had they remained on our territory, we would have co-opted them into this Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question wasn't answered. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have you done with the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would have a few questions in relation to the document. The document we were just discussing says something about food supplies. That's the first page. But before going to that, first, somewhere in the document "fighters" are mentioned. Fighters. Do I understand them to be fighters in the -- in your armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time it was still the Territorial Defence. The Army of Republika Srpska had not been formed yet. It was still the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 22nd of June. But my question was not whether it was TO or VRS on the 22nd of June. My question was whether it was your armed forces, that is, Serb, whether TO or VRS, I'm not -- were these Serb armed forces when you referred to "fighters"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part. For the most part. Almost 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, then, I take you back to the food supplies. Food will be supplied, there was a list of civilians, which -- and I'm talking about food supplies, that is under 2 (b) on the first page of this document. Lists of civilians were made, and food supplies amounting to 50 per cent of peacetime supplies were distributed to those on the lists. Then it says: "The basic criterion was to provide food for the families of fighters and refugees from the occupied territory." Now, you've explained to us that "fighters" were Serb fighters. You earlier explained to us that "refugees" were Serbs which had fled occupied territory. So they got food. Others didn't get food. At least it doesn't say anything about Muslims or -- it's just families of your own fighters and your refugees, they would get food, no one else. Or at least that was not the criterion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this same report, under 1, states that it was necessary to form local commune Crisis Staffs. There were ten local communes in Novo Sarajevo municipality, and there were local commune commissioners who were obliged to make lists. This was mostly a rural area. They had to make lists of families that needed assistance in this ratio as you mentioned. But the urban part, where Muslims and Croats lived, were also on the lists, according to different areas of the local communes. Nobody was excepted from receiving this aid. Everybody received what they were supposed to receive. Serb, Muslim, Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the names of the communes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the names of the communes you mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it says: Lukavica -- 1, Lukavica; 2, Tilava; Petrovici; Miljevici; Studenkovici; Kovacici, Gornji Kovacici, Donji; Jewish cemetery; Grbavica 1; Grbavica 2; Vraca 1; Vraca 2; Petrovacka Street. These were all local communes that had to keep records about those killed on the ground. They were the ones who would report on the situations first and, among other things, it was their duty to deal with humanitarian aid, the fair distribution of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I put to you that what you're telling us is not in line with what we see in this document, and I'm focussing now on the paragraph on food, which says: "Supplies were distributed to those on the lists," and who would be selected and what the criterion was, was a specific group. Now you are telling us that it was different than what is described here. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I claim is what I've just said. I said what I know for a fact. There was no discrimination at all. And in the last paragraph, when it says what the criterion was, was to feed refugees from occupied areas. They were mostly hailed from rural areas. Whereas the urban parts where Muslims and Croatians remained, I claim that they received the same things that I received in Vrace, which is also another urban part. And I guarantee that that was so. My neighbours, both Croats and Muslims - and you can check that because they are still alive, they are still there - they received the same rations as I did. They didn't receive a kilo more or less than the rest of us received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what the document tells us, but you say that is what happened in reality. Is that how I have to understand your -- because that leads me to my other question. You said there was no discrimination. Muslims could not feel unsafe. That's what you said. Due to the circumstances, there was no reason, I understand you to say, to feel unsafe. At the same time, you told us yesterday that part of the criminal activities - group of nine, including Batko - that they primarily targeted Muslims, and only after that, Serbs, and that no adequate action was taken in time. That's one thing you told us. Yesterday you also told us that there was a kind of a spontaneous agreement of exchange, but it wasn't real exchange but one group is moving to one side, another group moving to the other side of the confrontation lines; whereas, in documents, it is called "expulsion." It was reported in the Republika Srpska press as expulsion. Therefore, I'm struggling. I'm telling you to find out what explains your almost idyllic picture you're giving us and the documentary evidence which gives a different picture. And I found -- find that now again in relation to the food distribution, the food supplies, what I see on paper, is different from what you're telling us. So it's not only in relation to the food supplies but on the various subjects that you are giving a picture which is not the same as we find in these documents. Do you have an explanation for these differences in perception between you and those who were creating these press reports and these documents? Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, I tried to do that yesterday as well, but I didn't have the time to explain things properly. When it comes to the freedom of movement, i.e., non-discrimination, it was a war, so nobody could have been at ease, and that applied to Muslims, Croats and Serbs alike. But the care was the same for all three ethnicities given the situation we were in. It was a war, and according to the very definition of a war, nobody can feel at ease, nobody can feel relaxed. Second of all, regardless of this document, but this document doesn't say that Muslims and Croats didn't receive the same things as the Serbs, so even this document says that. Furthermore, you say that the media, the Serbian media, that is, said that the -- that the Muslims had been expelled. In the SRNA report on the 1st of October, which was only one day later, it doesn't say clearly. They were just opinions, there was just a summary of all the opinions of all of those who were interviewed about what they knew. I told you what I know and this is the most approximate description of the situation that took place on the 30th September. And I claim that Muslims were not expelled on that day. I had an occasion to see reports by the other side. None of the 300 Muslims who -- were cited there said that they were ill-treated or expelled by us, i.e., by the other side. They provided those statements on that same afternoon to some institutions, including UNPROFOR and the Red Cross, and they never said that it was due to ill-treatment that they crossed over or that they were expelled. And as for the exchange that I spoke about, I said that it was a gesture of good will and that Muslims were allowed to cross over as a gesture of good will. At the same time, on 15th of November, some 15 or 20 buses were allowed to cross over to the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're doing at this moment is rather repeating what you said before rather than explaining the apparent difference in the perception of those who created reports and press messages and your personal experience. I leave it to that. Mr. Lukic, I intervened when you said you had dealt with the document. Any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not on this document, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could take the break. Could you give us an estimate as to how much time you would need after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not if you continue helping me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I mean time you use, not time I use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Less than you use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know what I have on my mind what time I still want to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes. Okay, then we'll keep an eye on that. We first take a break, but not until after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, the Chamber observed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, meanwhile, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radan, let's continue. Yesterday the Prosecutor showed you a document which I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P352. P352.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will see that it is a notebook. We can see typed-up versions of that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in page 305 in B/C/S version and page 296 in English. These are not the same numbers I found earlier this morning in e-court and that version is used by the Defence. Let's return one page. Let's go back one page in B/C/S. I'm satisfied with the English page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now looking at B/C/S page 304 in e-court, and English 296 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. Now we have everything on the screen what we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor showed you the same document. It deals with a meeting that was held on the 11th of May, 1992. It says here that Colonel Kovacevic reported that he had been the brains of the weapons distribution for ten months and that, up to then, 69.000 Serbs had been armed. At that time, JNA members who responded to mobilisation calls, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exclusively Serbs. Because Alija Izetbegovic invited Muslims not to join the army or the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then in the following sentence, we read that Colonel Kovacevic asks for the chief of the -- chief of logistics to be kept in his position. In the first sentence of his presentation, you can see that he was the assistant commander for logistics, or PkPo, at the Command of the 2nd Military District. I don't know how much you know about military matters.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little. Let me tell you straight away that I don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know whether the procurement of weapons for units was within the purview of that man?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was a foot soldier. I never received any rank, so I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following document is P3030.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you please activate your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are conclusions. There is an accompanying letter, and it says that enclosed with the document, the requested assessment with annexes concerning the situation and problems in the territory of Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is being sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now go to the following page. The relevant period is March 1992 and the period preceding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in page 4, the same page that the Prosecutor showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English version, we need previous page, please. Can you go one page back in English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now at page 3 in the English version in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how this happened, but we need next page in -- in English. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean next to 3 or next to 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next to 3. It's -- it's top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Second. Where it says "second," yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was put to you yesterday, and it says here in this report: "The Serb people opted for Yugoslavia. If this option is not viable, only a confederal Bosnia and Herzegovina would be taken into account." "Quite simply a third option does not exist. "The leadership of the Serb people and the Serb people as a whole are fully prepared to -- for war, should the confederal option not be accepted." As for this war, to the best of your knowledge, were the Serbs preparing for it through attempts to ruin the common country, destroy it, or preserve it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, and I follow this carefully, reports from the Assembly, and I also attended some meetings, Serbs invested all of their energy to remain in Yugoslavia. If all of Yugoslavia could not remain, then Bosnia-Herzegovina should be in Yugoslavia nevertheless, and not in any variant whatsoever did they consider war then or did they opt for war. So all of this that is stated under number 2 is true. That is to say that every effort should be made to prevent a war. If a war were to happen, then we should defend ourselves because others wanted something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I ask the witness -- the document doesn't say: "If finally we are attacked." The document says: "The Serbian leadership and the Serbian people are fully prepared to wage a war." You're telling us something which is -- and I'm going back to what I said earlier, you're giving us a picture, right or wrong, I'm not giving any opinion about that, but which is totally different from what the text of this document says. "Fully prepared to wage a war." Wage a war is -- is to engage in a war and not if we are attacked, we have to defend ourselves. That's -- that's not the same language. I'm just pointing it to you so that you are aware that at least it may be perceived in a different way as you explain it, on the basis of the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Would you allow me just one sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document says that there are three options on the table. That is to say, if not a single one of the three is to be used, then the Serbs would be ready for war but they would never start it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not what the document says. It says if -- first of all, it says a third option simply does not exist. Therefore, it only gives two options. And then it says: "If what we consider appropriate is not accepted, we are ready -- we are fully prepared to wage a war." Now I'm not giving any opinion about whether it was justified or not, but the way in which you translate it seems to be not fully consistent with the language of that document. Unless you want to tell us, you would never start it because you would first try other peaceful means to settle the issues; but if you would be unsuccessful, that you would then wage a war, although you would not start by considering waging a war but you would start by seeking peaceful solutions. If that is what you want to tell us then -- then it seems to be more in line with the text which is before us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, just as you had put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is not the same as what you said but ... we now understand at least what you intended to say. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one thing. My question was not based only on this document. And I'll read to you, Your Honours, my question. My question, in line 10, page 26, says: "As for this war, to the best of your knowledge, not based on this document, were the Serbs preparing for it through attempts to ruin the common country or to save it," but we cannot see in the transcript "or to save it." So my question was based on the knowledge of this witness, so there was no need to bring him back strictly to this document. The Prosecution wanted to stick to this document. That was not my intention and that was not the question I posed to the witness and he was not answering that question. He was answering my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I asked him about his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may have misunderstood me --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't. Trust me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you understood me well, then there is no need to further explain, isn't there. Let's move on. What I did is I did put to the witness that what he answered to your question was inconsistent as far as language is concerned with what we find in a document. And that is a perfectly adequate question, I would say. Even if your question didn't take him to that document, I can take him to the document when he has answered your question and to see whether his answer is consistent with what we see in this document. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, may I draw your attention to line 17 of page 26. The witness in response to your question said: "So all of this that is stated under number 2 of the document." He related his answer to this document in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may also add, Mr. Lukic, you asked the question you asked after you showed the witness this document and referred him to what the Prosecutor said and that is why your question, broader as it might be, cannot be separated from this document because you relate it to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on, and let's try to get -- to get the complete answers to all the questions we may have. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your knowledge about the situation in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, is it restricted? And do you draw on all of your knowledge just from this document or is your knowledge about what happened in your municipality broader than what can be found in this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect do this document, this is the first time I see it, so I could not draw my knowledge on this document. I tried to draw my knowledge from many other documents and from the media and talks and broader and narrower knowledge. So, with all due respect, this document is not the only source of my information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in this context, I repeat what I said earlier. If the witness relies on other documentation, then, of course, the Chamber is interested to see that documentation so as to further support the evidence of this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to put any more questions to on the basis of this document because, as you said, this is the first time you see it. But on the other page, there is this math as to how many people were armed through corps, 62.000 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic repeat the numbers. This is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to corps or, rather, through corps, these were corps of the then-JNA, the 9th Corps, the 10th Corps, the 5th Corp, the 17th Corps, and the 4th Corps. The total number of people armed was 62.690 persons. And it is stated within the 4th Military District there is an additional 6.500 persons in volunteer units which brings to us a grand total of 62.190 and that is the number that is referred to in the report of Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt? May I interrupt you, Mr. Lukic? I'm lost. You said to the witness you're not going to further ask him about this document because it's the first time he sees. And then you are referring to figures and I'm not quite sure where you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention what this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same document that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is it on this page where we are?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Take us to the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to torture the witness. I wanted to cut it short, but we can go to the page. It's page 5 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read it, the Chamber is entitled to know where you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 5 in B/C/S. I hope it's the same page in English version. It's the next page in English [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 6, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. We can see numbers, one below the other. Yeah, now we have it in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What were you saying about the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under (d), number of men in the corps zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page in B/C/S? It's not the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page probably 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 5 in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 6 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Must be -- must be 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 7 in B/C/S, sorry. It was double pages. Then the next one again. There is some double pages in this document, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In e-court, it's supposed to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we have it on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page -- page 8 in B/C/S e-court. Let me just -- Mr. Lukic, you referred to weapons being distributed through the corps, whereas I find JNA distributed so many weapons, and the SDS --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- okay. We'll carefully read what you have drawn our attention to. But this is not just about distribution of weapons through the corps. It is the number of men in the zones of responsibility of the corps, and it apparently refers to distribution of weapons by the JNA, without further details as how they were distributed by the JNA, and by the SDS. And, further, it says something about the position of volunteers, and that the volunteer units are not part of the JNA and the TO establishment structure. So -- so there's a lot of information apparently there which one would need to analyse very carefully before one could draw any conclusions from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's why I just draw your attention to this page, and I know that I cannot ask this witness nothing about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Perhaps at a later moment then you may further elaborate on what is found in this part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document we need is P353. [Interpretation] This is a notebook. We need the page that the Prosecution showed you: B/C/S page 307. And, in the English version, page 308. [In English] I was checking the handwritten version, and obviously in B/C/S the pages are not the same. We have to go back one page in B/C/S version. Yeah, that's it. We need middle of the page where Koljevic is reporting this meeting. It's recorded that it's meeting from 10th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were told -- well, it says here, Koljevic is saying: "Batko is terrorising Grbavica, must be arrested."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, arrested. Through this sentence -- I think it's clear. I don't even think I have to ask you. I think it's clear that the army is not giving assistance or support to this Batko who is being discussed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you're telling to the witness it's clear and that you don't have to ask questions, then you should move on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I have another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But that's not what happened. Okay. You have another question. Could you please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, perhaps, if the Trial Chamber thinks I should put that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When somebody asks for an arrest, is that support or is that an attempt to work against that person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO RADAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything here fits in with the indications or the intentions that we had as we were working on the ground. It's all synchronised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my second question, actually. You anticipated it. We are now finished with this document. Mr. Radan, thank you very much. Even though I already said it before that I didn't have any questions, now I really mean it. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Have the questions triggered any need for further questions, Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This means -- one second, please. This means, Mr. Radan, that we are at the end of your examination as a witness. I'd like to thank you very much for -- first of all, for coming to The Hague, and, second, for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties or by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the Defence will be invited to call its next witness, I would like to deal with a few procedural matters. Perhaps then take a break and then start the examination of the next witness after the break. I first would like to deal with a few matters in relation to the revised witness list which was filed by the Defence. The witness and exhibit lists were filed a few minutes after the deadline that was set by the Chamber, and they received, as a result, the filing date of the 19th of May, 2014, but despite this, the Chamber accepts this late filing. For some of the witnesses who are indicated to testify as Rule 94 bis witness, that is, experts, the Chamber wondered whether the gist of their evidence is really their expertise or, rather, their factual observations. I just, in this context, note entries numbers 36, 51, 80, 83, 104, and 184. But I leave the matter for the time being in the hands of the parties. The Chamber notes that the Defence - and that is in line with the Chamber's Rule 73 ter decision - has cut down the times for examination-in-chief for many witnesses. Other than removing Prosecution [sic] witnesses from its list, the Defence has removed Witnesses GRM086, GRM120, and GRM313, but then replaced these with two new witnesses, GRM337 and GRM338. The Defence has not significantly reduced the number of witnesses, and the Chamber wonders whether this may also have led to somewhat unrealistically low estimates for some of the witnesses. Of course, we do encourage the efficient examination of witnesses but just by striking minutes, you have not yet shortened a testimony of a witness. The Chamber further notes that the time claimed for expert witnesses - I'm referring to GRM036, GRM049, GRM083, GRM087, GRM109, GRM134, and GRM140, GRM191, and GRM193 - is 30 minutes for each of these experts. If that means that the Defence will mainly rely on expert reports and would have no further questions for those experts, then, of course, it may be a very efficient way of proceeding. If, however, it would be on the back of your mind also to examine those witnesses on perhaps sometimes complex expert issues, then one could wonder whether 30 minutes is a realistic estimate for the time needed for that, and the Chamber would like the Defence to thoroughly think about such issues. For Witness GRM045, the witness list indicates an estimated time for examination-in-chief of 30 minutes. However, the mode of testimony for this witness is Rule 92 bis, and the Defence is invited to clarify this contradiction. For the last item, I'd like to discuss -- I would like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. For the public record, the Chamber has just issued an oral decision whereby it ordered, proprio motu, pursuant to Rule 75(A) of the Rules, that the testimony of Witness RM019 remains in closed session. We take a break, and I also take it that the Defence will be ready to call its next witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will take a break, and we resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution would like to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, just briefly. In line with our earlier discussions about Rule 90(E), I do inform the Chamber that this witness did receive a 90(E) warning when he testified before the Karadzic case. With respect to my examination of him, I do intend to ask him about his involvement in shelling Scheduled Incident G4. He was the legal advisor for the brigade during the shelling incident. We'll ask him specific questions about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might not be wise to give him, then, that warning in the beginning, in a general sense. But if you would indicate when you would like me to inform the witness -- well, whether it's a warning or whether it's informing him, that's -- that's two ways of saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Right. I will do that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, I leave it to you whether you find any reason to -- to at an earlier stage put this to the witness. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I already -- I -- in addition to the decision in relation to Witness RM019 I delivered before the break, in order to avoid any confusion, I'd like to add that we decided, proprio motu, to -- that the testimony of this witness remains in closed session but also includes pseudonym. That remains as well. Second, the Chamber received information from the Prosecution that, in view of the information they received from the briefing by the Defence, that they extended their time estimate for cross-examination from two to two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mijatovic. Could I invite you to stand for a second. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me greet you and I would kindly thank you for the invitation to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Defence invited you. There's no need to say that. If you would just make that solemn declaration, that would be it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mijatovic. Please be seated. Mr. Mijatovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic, and you'll find him to your left. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Good day to you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your name, including your last name, for the record.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Nikola Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to call up in e-court 65 ter number 1D01607.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look together at the first page of the document in the Serbian original, can you tell me if you can confirm whose signature appears at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the last page in e-court in both versions, that should be page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, there's also a signature and a date on this page. Can you tell me if you recognise the same?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: This is my signature. And the date is 16 May 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, subsequent to signing this statement, sir, did you have occasion to review the statement in the Serbian language for purposes of verifying if there were any corrections or additions required?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I had an occasion, and together with you, I made some additions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could first turn to page 2 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S of this document, 1D01607.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to focus, sir, on the second paragraph and the discussion of the neighbour that warned of plans to murder you. And if we could, at the same time, look at paragraph 5 of the statement, where it also says that a neighbour told you of a planned murder of you in your automobile. And I'd like to ask you to clarify are these the same incidents involving the same neighbour?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: It was not the same neighbour. In that case, the young man was from a mixed marriage. His father was a Serb. And in the second case, the gentleman was a Muslim, and if you want me to tell you his name, I don't want to do it publicly. The man helped me, I don't want to discredit him and complicate his life. I'm very grateful to him for having done what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could briefly go into private session for the purposes of getting the individual's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, now if we could look at paragraph number 4 on the same page in both versions. The harassment of Serbian children based on their Serb ethnicity that you describe here, what is the basis of this testimony? What the basis of your knowledge of the same?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: My children, my three children, my three daughters, suffered harassment. They would be harassed by my neighbours, and that started in 1990 and 1991. The children of my other friends and relatives fared the same, but particularly my children were involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look at paragraph 7 together.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That can be found in e-court at page 3 of the B/C/S and page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, in the statement, sir, you are mentioning a primary school 1st Maj on Cetinjska Street, and I note that the Serbian version mentions a machine-gun nest or "mitraljesko gnezdo" while the English translation mentions a sniper nest. What can you tell us in relation to this? Which accords with your recollection of what was present approximately 150 metres from this school on Cetinjska Street?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, there were both, both a sniper nest and a machine-gun nest at the beginning of the war. There was also a mortar position nearby, and -- and that's the truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we are at this paragraph, can you provide any further details about your source of the information contained herein about the 1st Maj school being used as a makeshift prison for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The source of that information was my sister-in-law -- or, rather, my wife's sister. Her son, Srdjan Lazic was brought in merely because he had my videocamera. And first he was taken to the MUP. He was a 15-year-old child at the time but he was tall. He was already very tall at the time. And he was first taken to the MUP, which was across the street from my building, and then to the school some 100 metres away from the MUP. And he told me that he had seen that a Serb had his head cut off and those who cut his head off with a sword cursed his Chetnik mother. He saw that people had their limbs broken. There was a case when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- could I, first of all, invite you to slow down so that the interpreters can follow your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, a lot of information comes as a kind of a waterfall. Could you please try to get some structure in it. Because it's unclear whose head was cut off and whether that happened at that moment or -- well, it's pretty unclear. Please listen to Mr. Ivetic's questions and try to focus your answers on what he asks you because the source of the information apparently was the son of the sister of your wife. That was the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you clarify for us what exactly it was that the son of the sister of your wife told you took place at the school and to whom, by whom?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That school had already been transformed into a prison at the beginning of the war. Muslims had cut a Serb's head off. He concluded that he was a Serb because they cursed his Chetnik mother. And also another Serb had his limbs broken by paramilitary formations, the so-called Green Berets and the Patriotic League, who were already active in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now turn to paragraph 23. That is to be found on page 5 in the English and page 6 in the Serbian in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek clarification on one or two items. Do I understand that this 15-year-old boy was present when the head of a Serb was cut off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if his mother had not intervened, I suppose that he would have ended up in the same way. She went there, she screamed and cried and wailed and pleaded, and she managed to have him released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apparently his mother was nearby as well. Do you know the identity of the Serb whose head was cut off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at paragraph 23 of your statement. That should be on the screen before you, sir. And I'd like to ask you: Does this paragraph accurately and fully state your reasons for not believing document P2795 from the Galic trial, or do you wish to add some further detail?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was very familiar with that line at the time. Across from that line were the combat positions of the so-called BiH Army, i.e., the Muslim army. They were across the road from our positions. What was typical of that part of town was that across the road from our facilities, and I'm talking about Nedzarici, was that those were 5- to 7-storey buildings whereas the constructions in Nedzarici were two storeys high at the most. Throughout the war there were no civilians in this neighbourhood because it would not have been logical to expect any of the civilians to walk between two combat lines --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask for some clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Ivetic, we are apparently listening to a comment of the witness on a P exhibit in the Galic case. Is the Chamber aware of the content of that? Have we been provided with it? Because it's difficult for us to understand, not that he doesn't believe it, but he has doubts as the statement says, which is not exactly the same, but how could we follow this evidence if we are not aware of what the underlying document says?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the statement as it was in the Karadzic case, this particular selection. And, unfortunately, we do not have in the JDB from the Galic case this particular exhibit so as to -- we have the testimony from the Karadzic case where they referred to it. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you seriously presenting us a comment of the witness in a statement on a document which you say you don't have?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is the witness statement as was given to me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are responsible for the presentation of evidence, Mr. Ivetic. You can't hide behind those who have given you a statement. I mean, if I see it at first sight, you could have asked those who provide you with the statement for which you primarily bear responsibility to have it adduced as evidence. But I do understand that you don't have it. So most likely then you would not understand what the witness's testimony is either or on the basis of other unknown to us transcripts. Mr. Groome, are you able to assist or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, I believe there's a typographical error in the statement. It references P2795 from the Galic case. I'd encourage Mr. Ivetic to check the transcript of the Galic case at T-16856. I believe the correct number is P2759. And, Your Honour, we have looked at that and it is P1079 in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- one second, please. Yes, if that assists -- at least we could have a look at P1079 in this case and see whether it makes sense and whether there's a fair chance that we're talking about the same document. Meanwhile, please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in relation to the positions of the ABiH that you have identified, where were they in relation to the 7- to 10-storey buildings identified in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Our positions were some 50 metres away. Some were -- some of them were even closer. Sometimes only a street divided us. I'm specifically talking about Alipasino Polje --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking about the ABiH positions, not the VRS positions. Where were the ABiH positions in relation to the 7- to 10-storey buildings?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: In Alipasino Polje, in military field and Dobrinja 5, those were the high-rise buildings that surrounded Nedzarici. Those buildings housed the positions of the Muslim army, the so-called BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 28 of your statement, which is to be found on page 7 in both languages, you have identified a military headquarters and a 120-millimetre mortar near the site of the incident in question in Hrasnica. Are those the only two military installations in Hrasnica that were known to you, or are there others?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: There were others as well. I'm surprised that this has been omitted. I've already told you so, because I mentioned them. The brigade in Hrasnica had some 80 heavy weapons, three tanks, five APCs. It had 105-millimetre howitzers, 120-millimetre howitzers, 100-millimetre cannons. I personally observed a multi-rocket-launcher and I ordered my men to fire that rocket-launcher in Hrasnica. In other words, there were a lot more weapons and assets than are mentioned here. I've already spoken about that. I believe that due to speed those facts have been omitted from my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how large is the area of Hrasnica? That is to say, the area where all these military installations were located that you have just listed for us.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The area could be 3 to 4 kilometres long and approximately 2 kilometres wide. It was a small neighbourhood. It was not a town or -- it was not a village either. It was just a neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, apart from the corrections and clarifications we've talked about today, do you stand behind your written statement, as we have in e-court?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you were to be asked the same questions today about the same topics as in your statement, would you provide the same answers, in substance, subject only to the corrections and additions that we've gone through in court?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration in the courtroom, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of this statement, subject to the clarifications --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Wait for me to finish my question. Subject to the clarifications and corrections we went through?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honours, at this time I would tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be something wrong. Your microphone seems to be activated, nevertheless we don't hear. Could you please restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. At this time I would tender the statement of the witness, 1D01607, into evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
