utterances.text: Your Honour, the proofing note that we received on Wednesday evening listed a number of corrections, one of which seems significant that has not been dealt with. Can I draw Mr. Ivetic's attention to paragraph 11 of the statement. Has to do with a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 11, sir - and that should be on page 4 in both versions - here you have several dates and several positions that you held in the brigade. Are all the positions that you held in the brigade accurately depicted here, along with the dates that you held those positions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: This is obviously a mistake. I was the chief of security in the Ilidza Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, could you speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, i.e., towards the end of May 1992, I was seriously wounded. I suffered a bullet wound. I was clinically dead. I was treated for three months in the hospital, so it could not have been in 1992. It must a typo. This was the same period of 1993. That's why I said that this should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you, sir, after spending time in the hospital, to what position in the brigade were you first assigned, and when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from the hospital, I was assigned to the logistics unit. I spent several months there. After rehabilitation, when I was feeling better, I became the assistant brigade commander for information, morale, and religious issues. After that, I became chief of security in the Ilidza Brigade. And then sometime in July 1993 -- or, rather, in September 1994, I apologise, I became the Chief of Staff and deputy commander of the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the date when you would have become the assistant for information, morale, and religious matters in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: This could have been in November 1992. In any case, it was before the new year of 1992 [as interpreted]. It probably was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to becoming the chief of security in the brigade, do you -- am I correct -- could you tell us that date? It's a little unclear from your answer what that date was.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: It could have been sometime in March or April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm not quite sure, but at page 55, lines 22 to 23, whether the witness wanted to say before the new year of 1993 or of 1992. Because previously he said it was November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, are you able to assist Judge Moloto with clarifying your answer. Was it the new year of 1992 or 1993 that you meant to reference?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Before the new year 1993, which means that this was in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, apart from this further clarification, do you stand by your witness statement as it is written?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Subject to the solemn declaration you have taken, do you affirm that the answers therein are truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I confirm that my answers are truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D01607 into evidence as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Groome. Before we decide -- Witness, could you tell me, you commented in paragraph 23 on alleged activity in the home for the blind, which was contained in a document that was shown to you. Could you tell us what exactly that document with which you disagreed, what it said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was in the Galic case, when General Stanislav Galic was being tried, my commander, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I remember an instance when they talked about a guy. There was no name. The guy wasn't identified, or the part of the body where he was wounded. There was just a report that some young man was injured -- wounded, that he was taken to the hospital and given medical assistance. The point there was to accuse us, the Serbian side, of sniper fire against civilians. And I said, well, the name of the person is not cited. It doesn't say where he was wounded. There's no mention of the weapon that wounded him. I remember that case very well. I was here. I don't remember if it was the same courtroom or not. But I think that perhaps I also talked about the situation, the description about that event, and that's why I said that I just doubted all of the things that were said then about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have -- you said it was about a -- the name of the person was not cited but it was about a young man which was wounded. I'm -- what I found -- find as most likely the only possible reference in P1079 is that reference is made to a Bosnian civilian, male, age 48 - of course, people may wish still to be young at the age of 48 - but wounded by SA fire, alleged to be fire at Kovaci. Therefore, I do not see any reference to the home of the blind. Was that mentioned in that report on which you commented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kovaci. I know about a part of town that is on the other side of Sarajevo. Kovaci is in Bascarsija. And that case that you're talking about has nothing do with the area of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade where I was. If you know Sarajevo and where Bascarsija is, then this is above Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know where Bascarsija is. I'm totally lost as far as paragraph 23 is concerned and since the witness says that he would give the same answer -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can assist, Your Honour. I believe what the witness -- I think the witness's memory is failing him on what happened in Galic, but having read the Galic transcript, I believe if you look at e-court page 4 and if you look at item 24(B), I think that's the part that was relevant in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 24(B). Let me have a look. 24, and then B. Let me see. Let me read, then, what is found in the document on which you apparently have commented. It says: The command, or commander, COMD, 1st BN, which stands for abbreviation -- I don't know whether it's a brigade or -- BN ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Battalion of the BSA," which stands for Bosnian Serb Army, I take it, "Ilidza Brigade, admitted the sniping by Bosnian Serb Army from BP 859578 (house for blind people). He promised that there would be no more sniping from that place." It doesn't say anything about a young person having been wounded. It says something about a statement given by the commander of the Ilidza -- of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade who apparently had admitted the sniping by the Bosnian Serb Army from the house for the blind people. You now say: I personally doubt it. What do you doubt? That he said so, or do you doubt that there was sniping activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm hearing it for the first time that he admitted it. Secondly, I don't know -- I mean, I stand by what I said when the case was presented to me. I think we need to find that. I don't know if it's the same incident, but I know 100 per cent that, at that time, it was about a young man who was wounded. He was not named. They didn't say where he was wounded. Just that he was wounded and taken to the hospital. I don't know. As for this commander, you can ask him what he saw and what he said. I wasn't there. I cannot confirm or deny what is said. I'm talking about the event that I asked about, that it was impossible from our side to hit a civilian because the buildings in front of us had 7 to 10 storeys, and you cannot believe that civilians were walking around in front of our positions. I think that you would agree with me. I mean, the lines. I mean, we would be divided by a street, so you can imagine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- so these are conclusions you've drawn. Because the document, at least the part I read, doesn't say anything about civilians. It's -- just says "sniper activity," not referring in any way to civilians yet. But you say it's illogical and therefore it can't be true. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. It was about the incident that I was questioned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we do not know at this moment what it is. But now at least it becomes a bit more clear what it is all about. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number for the 92 ter witness statement would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1607 receives number D468, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D468 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, I noticed that one of the persons who interviewed the witness was counsel, Mr. Stojanovic. So, therefore, to say, "that is how I received it," he is seated 1 and a half metre behind you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to tender at this time two associated exhibits. 1D02295 and 1D02296.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2295 receives number D469, Your Honours. And document 1D2296 receives number D470, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D469 and D470 are admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time I would like to read a summary of the Rule 92 ter evidence. I have during proofing explained the purpose of this summary to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikola Mijatovic lived in the Alipasino Polje part of Sarajevo with his family until neighbours told him about multiple plots to kill him because he was a prominent Serb living there for about ten years. He and his family left Sarajevo in April 1992 as a result. Before he left, Mr. Mijatovic noted information received from others that Bosnian Muslims were organising the distribution of weapons to those considered reliable. He personally witnessed a truck of rifles that was parked in front of his apartment, which he reported to the police, but he suspects the Bosnian Muslim police officers told the truck driver to hide the same. He noted that the demeanour of Bosnian Muslim neighbours became hostile towards Serbs before he departed Sarajevo and that even Serb children were abused due to their ethnicity. Upon departing Sarajevo, the witness became part of the Ilidza Brigade, eventually becoming chief of security and then Chief of Staff. His testimony is that the ABiH utilized civilian schools to manufacture grenades and launchers. His testimony is that the ABiH side shelled the power transfer station which covered both Ilidza and Sarajevo, cutting off power, and then falsely blaming the Serbs. His testimony is that the ABiH often shelled Ilidza from near where UNPROFOR was situated, despite complaints about the same. According to his information, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps suffered from a severe shortage of artillery and mortar ammunition. It is for these reasons that the corps was compelled to use modified aerial bombs. The trajectory of these bombs was predetermined and could be controlled. As with any other type of guided weapons, there was a chance of minimum deviation due to meteorological conditions. The objective for using modified aerial bombs was defence, to defend themselves against ABiH attacks, and prevent a breakthrough by the ABiH through the lines and thus prevent an ABiH massacre of the civilian population of Ilidza. No one in his brigade nor, as far as he knows, in the corps command intended to terrorise civilians in part of the city controlled by Muslim forces. He received reports that Muslims were also using modified aerial bombs. The witness also discusses the incident G10, noting that certain ABiH military targets were in that part of Hrasnica, including a command of the BH Army, and a 120-millimetre mortar. As to G13, the witness points out this was during a fierce Bosnian Muslim offensive when both sides were actively shooting. Than completes a summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 4 of your statement and paragraphs 15 and 16, here, sir, you are talking about the Muslim side giving false information to the UN that the Serbs were targeting civilians, and you give an account of when the ABiH shelled a power transfer station and then blamed the Serbs for -- for -- for cutting off electricity. I would like to look at document 1D02085 with you. Sir, if you could focus on this document, it's dated 13 December 1992, and it's a report of your brigade signed by the commander. If we look at item number 1, does this appear to be related to the attack of the power transfer station that you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: This refers to this case, although there were a number of cases of shelling damage of this Muslim transformer station. This is a station that Sarajevo was supplied through, as well as Serbian Ilidza, as well as the waterworks. So if you hit the station and the oil is lost, then there would be no water for Serbian Ilidza or for other parts of Sarajevo, in the city and on the outskirts of town. So everything went through this transformer station, and it was something that was used for constant pressure and for deceiving the public because what they wanted was to create the impression that the Serbs were constantly inflicting terror. But actually our people were wounded near the station. When this happened I remember very well. As far as I remember, there were 30 tonnes of oil that leaked from the station, and it's something that we were storing near the airport. We had received this from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch from whom --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is how the transformer station was supplied with this oil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. One second, please. Could we first seek -- you told us about the 30 tonnes of oil that leaked from the station and you had received this from whom or from what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was personally there. I went when this happened, and so, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You spoke so quickly that the interpreters did not hear what you said. "We -- we had received this from," and then they failed to hear what you then said. Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received the oil from UNPROFOR, the oil that we used once the transformer station was repaired. We got it through them because it was impossible for us to obtain it because of the money, transport, and all these things. But throughout that whole period, the water supply system was inoperative as well. Nothing could work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I asked you is to repeat from whom you got that oil. The simple answer, therefore, is from UNPROFOR. Carefully listen to the next question Mr. Ivetic will put to you and focus your answer on the question, rather than telling us the whole story of the war, which I can imagine is on your mind, but you're here to give answers to these questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Muslim side offer any assistance in repairing the transfer station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no offer of help.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in item 1 of this document, there is discussion that on this occasion the ABiH also struck the hospital and other civilian facilities. Does this document accord with your recollection of this incident?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I remember it vividly because this shelling was a specific case, and that's why I remember it. There was a policeman, Zeljko Knezovic. In the same day, his father and mother were killed, and they died at the Zica hospital where the civilians were being treated because of this. There were other wounded and other people who died as well, but I just happen to remember this particular case of Zeljko. There were other such cases, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm a bit lost again by looking at this document. Because you asked a question in relation to the Muslim side providing false information to UNPROFOR. Could you assist me in finding that in the report by the Ilidza Brigade Command under number 1, because as far as I can see, it doesn't say anything about reporting to UNPROFOR so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's the statement of the witness in paragraph 16 where he says: "On this occasion, the Muslim side falsely informed the UNPROFOR that we were the ones who had cut off their electrical supply."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. Yes, yes, I misread. I focussed on 15, and I should have carefully read 16 as well. Nevertheless, the reporting here -- oh, you just wanted to say this was the incident related to what the witness said about the reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us anything about the report itself? How did they report it to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer? Mr. Ivetic, should I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should answer because I put the question to you, yes. Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I apologise. I'm sorry. The usual line of reporting of UNPROFOR would go from the battalion up to the brigade level. From the brigade, up to the corps level. The corps would inform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about how usually reporting went on. What I'm asking you is what you could tell us exactly about the way in which the Muslim side reported this incident to UNPROFOR. What did they exactly say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They told UNPROFOR that we had shelled the transformer station briefly. But actually it was a total lie. When the UNPROFOR members went to the scene --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep it to that. I -- have you seen a written report, or what -- how do you know exactly that they blamed you for this shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because UNPROFOR, when they came to us, they told us this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. You were told by UNPROFOR. And what did UNPROFOR, then, exactly say they had reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They said that we had fired at the transformer station. But then when we went to the scene, experts for mortar weapons and artillery weapons, together with UNPROFOR, determined that the shots - there were a number of them - the shots had come from the Muslim side. And since there were UNPROFOR observers next to all of our weapons, all we did was say to them: Well, why don't you just ask your people if we had fired from anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, last question in this context. This transformer station, was it situated in an area controlled by the Bosnian Serb Army or by the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. It was on our territory, on Serb territory. In the area of Blazuj. That was the precise location. Close to the Bosna river source. And that's what the station was called, Vrelo Bosne. But then it was exposed to fire from the Muslim side from all directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were blamed for firing at an installation which they said was on your own -- of the territory -- territory controlled by yourself. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But that was not the first false accusation. It was one in a series of such false accusations by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would tender 1D02085 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is Mr. Ivetic able to provide any provenance information? I can't seem to locate where the document came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There appears to be a stamp from the Galic case in the upper right-hand corner of the B/C/S original. It was disclosed to us in that form and the translation appears to be a CLSS translation. So I would surmise that this was used in the Galic case. We got it off the EDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask that it be marked for identification to just give us an opportunity to investigate where the document came from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections, I take it, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Merely technical verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2085 receives number D471, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification. I apologise. It's time for me to take a break, I think. We'll take a break, Witness, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness, Your Honour, I can also give Mr. Groome additional information about 1D02085. That was admitted as Exhibit D02510 in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Groome, that we'll hear within the next two or three court days about your position about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could return to the written statement, Exhibit D00468. And if we can look at page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, sir, I can introduce it. In this paragraph, paragraph 6, you talk about the lorry filled with weapons that you ran into outside of your apartment building. And I would like to ask you if this is the only such incident that you have personal knowledge of near your home of weapons being shipped clandestinely prior to the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's not the only case. There were other cases. There was me and then I reported that to the police station opposite my house. This other case was when I was with Boro Ivanisevic, my neighbour from the 11th floor. The third case was this information from my very own brother. At that time, he was a senior inspector at the police station in Hadzici. That is the first station, the first municipality right next to Ilidza. And they caught this -- or, rather, captured this truck full of ammunition and weapons, Muslim, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take them one by one sir. Could I first ask you to provide us the details of the other incident that you identify in reference to your neighbour from the 11th floor.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: We saw this vehicle then. As far as I can remember, it was a Zastava; 3 and a half tonnes. You could see that inside there were wooden boxes with military equipment. I mean, rifles are kept in boxes like that. So that was that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now can you tell us of the details of the incident involving your brother, the police inspector at Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: A subordinate policeman of his, Camur, an ethnic Serb, he was on duty near the quarry. There is this quarry near the exit out of Hadzici and then policemen were often on duty there. On that day, he realised that there was a freight truck there escorted by a police vehicle but the police vehicle did not have rotating lights. And that intrigued him and that made him suspicious, didn't have rotating lights, and any police vehicle would have to have that when escorting this kind of truck and also they couldn't have been on in that case. And then he stopped these colleagues and said: Who are you escorting and what? And they said: Flour. And then he said: Since when do people give a police escort to flour? And then that made him suspicious and he lifted this tarpaulin and then he saw these boxes with rifles. He informed my brother and the commander of the police station and -- you used a Motorola to inform my brother, who was his superior, and also the commander of the police station, a Serb, because he knew that these were Muslims. He recognised them. And also this police escort, these policemen were too. And then the secretary of the committee came and the president of the municipality. They were Muslims. And these guys were locked up there. I mean, it was right there on this spot. They convinced them that they should all go back to the police station in Hadzici and that's about 700 metres -- that is about 700 to 800 metres from the police station, that they should go back and then the policemen would take this vehicle and go back to the station. And these people obeyed them because they didn't want to create a conflict right there on the spot, and they believed that that is what would happen ultimately. But there were no -- there were no divisions yet, concrete ones, between the policemen, Serbs and Muslims. The Serbs believed that the Muslims would honour their word.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the end of the day, what happened to that lorry that was discovered with the rifles in the escort of a police vehicle without rotating lights?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it simply disappeared. This truck never came to the police station. It just went along and went to the Muslim population that it had been intended for in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what you're telling us is what you heard from your brother, or do you have any personal knowledge of these events? That is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about this from my brother and his colleague, Tiho Glavas. He was the commander of the station in Hadzici. It's not a secret so I can mention his name. And also directly from this Camur who stopped all of this. So all of this is first-hand, if you can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would call it second-hand if you hear it from them, but let's not argue about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just ask for a clarification. You said in a previous answer: Well, the truck simply disappeared. How do you know that it went to the Muslim population if it just disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because of what I said. The Muslim policemen were escorting this vehicle and also this freight vehicle, the driver and the person accompanying him all of -- all of them were Muslims. So it's a very realistic assumption, that they went to where it had been intended for and to whom it had been intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So I take it, it's your assumption? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to draw your focus on the time-period after the war already began. And do you have any personal knowledge of weapons or ammunition being clandestinely transported to the Bosnian Muslims during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I have several personal experiences of ammunition being transported to Muslims. One of these cases was when we stopped a UNHCR convoy. When we lifted the container there on the trailer, and underneath, as far as I can remember now, about 30 ammunition boxes were found there for anti-aircraft guns, Brownings, and sniper ammunition was found as well and infantry ammunition too. This is one case. Now, there was this other case. I was personally present when, in this convoy that was taking humanitarian aid to Sarajevo, we also found ammunition for snipers and for Brownings and even some weapons too. The next case was --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Finish the next case. Then I'd like to ask you a question about additional information about this.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally also realised that UNPROFOR vehicles that had Brownings on them, say, 30 APCs, would get in and they would all have these heavy machine-guns, and when they would leave town, even during a routine control, military policemen told us, and I personally saw some of these situations, ten or 15 Brownings would be missing in a convoy of 30 vehicles. Now let me tell you about this proportion, where they disappeared, these Brownings. We asked them and they told us that Muslims seized them in the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like -- I'd like to go back to the -- you talked about stopping UNHCR convoys. On how many occasions were you able to confirm that UNHCR convoys were being used to clandestinely transport weapons to the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Several times. But twice we confirmed this. By having these TV cameras there that were on the spot. Actually, we managed to get them there and then they managed to film this. So several times. But then we have these two documented cases, as we call it. I would sometimes be out in the field. Then the military police would find this, even without me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can I just clarify one point before it disappears from the screen. Sir, at page -- at page 73, starting from line 22, you say: "Yes, I personally also realised that UNPROFOR vehicles that had Brownings on them, say 30 APCs would get in ..." I'm not quite sure how the APCs are connected with the UNPROFOR vehicles. Can you explain that a little bit? I just see that little phrase, "say, 30 APCs," getting thrown into that sentence and I'm not quite sure what it means, how the two are connected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are APCs, transporters that UNPROFOR takes. No dilemma. I really don't understand. I'm so sorry. What is it that you don't understand? These are APCs, transporters of UNPROFOR that usually had Brownings or anti-aircraft guns mounted on them. But there were APCs that had anti-aircraft guns of 20-millimetres. However, these were those that were supposed to transport personnel and they had Brownings on them. Brownings are heavy machine-guns or, rather, anti-aircraft guns, but then they can also be used to fire at artillery -- at infantry too, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a follow-up question about the same answer you gave. You say you personally also realised that UNPROFOR vehicles that had Brownings on them, say, 30 APCs, would get in, and they would all have these heavy machine-guns. I do understand that they were equipped with these guns. And when they would leave town, even during a routine control, military policemen told us, and you saw some of these situations, ten or 15 Brownings would be missing in a convoy of 30 vehicles. Is it your testimony that it's your assumption, that since they did not have all those Brownings on these vehicles when they left town, that they must have been left with the Muslims? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Mr. President. Precisely. Because we checked the vehicles, and they were not in the vehicles. And then we wrote written reports about that to our command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the -- the factual part of your statement is you saw APCs leaving town without these heavy machine-guns mounted on it. That's the facts that you observed. What explained that, whether they were under repair, or whether they were taken by Muslims, or whether they were just -- you -- do you have any knowledge about that, or is it just your observation that you saw them without these Brownings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were not being repaired. Because UNPROFOR soldiers themselves told us that, allegedly, Muslims had seized these weapons from them in town. This information was obtained from UNPROFOR soldiers. So there's no assumption there that they were being repaired. Allegedly they were seized from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They were stolen, if I understand you -- well, they were stolen by the Muslims from UNPROFOR. Yes -- well, that clarifies part of your answer. Then the other matter is the recorded incidents of smuggling weapons. You said two were recorded. The others were not recorded. Do you mean to say not recorded by a camera, or were they not recorded, were they not documented in the hierarchical lines and -- I mean, the two you observed yourself, Mr. -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good question. And let me explain. Twice I said that we recorded this, as far as I know. I happened to be there when we captured them, if I can put it this way. Actually when we caught them smuggling for Muslims, ammunition. That was filmed on camera. Then there was this other case when this would be recorded in writing, and our superior command would always be informed about that. So it's not that it was unrecorded. It was recorded but in writing, not on camera. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then complaints were lodged, I take it, at the UNPROFOR Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A higher command, yes, that was authorised to have relations with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I'd like to take look video. 1D00358. Transcripts have been provided to the booths. We have, I believe, played this video with prior witnesses during the Prosecution case so I don't know whether we still need to do it twice. Shall we play --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that where it is recorded how the contraband was detected in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before, the number of the ID has not been recorded. Can you just make sure we've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, perhaps a good compromise would be if you would just play it and we can -- of course the text spoken can be -- it is in evidence already, I do understand, but it refreshes our memory as --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not in evidence yet. It's was only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been played but not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it was played with respect to Prosecution witnesses who could not offer confirmation of the location, the date or the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it would make sense if this witness would have been present at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's have a look at it. Should it be played twice? Is there any -- is it text spoken --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is text spoken, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Twice. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There seems to be an issue with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because it's moving up and down. The picture is not showing exactly -- of course, we saw a few -- a few pictures where apparently ammunition was shown to the camera. Now we see different pictures. We've seen this before. What's the length of the whole of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Two minutes, Your Honours. Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we've looked at it for more than two minutes already. I -- yes, I don't know -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Certainly if Mr. Ivetic wants to go forward, I would have no objection to him reopening his direct examination when he can sort out the technical problems. Can I ask, last time this was shown, at transcript 3836, the Defence said they were still trying to determine the date of the video, has that been done yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness is hopefully the one who can provide us that information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we -- we want to see it in its entirety later but we could already ask the witness whether he recognises anything he has seen. Witness, this video, there are some technical problems, but I take it that you were able to at least see something, boxes being opened, ammunition being -- in those boxes. Does -- have you been present during -- at this moment at that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was present -- I was providing a statement there because journalists asked me questions. Since that was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. I take it step by step. Does that mean that we could see you in the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, not in this clip, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in this clip. Do you remember where this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I do. It was in Ilidza, very close to Kasindolska Street. It happened in the spring of 1993. I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any further details? Spring could still cover three months, but do you know whether -- what month it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this could have been in late March or mid-April. As far as I can remember, that would have been the period. There were thousands of events in the war, so it's very hard to remember the exact dates. And there were very many similar cases. They were cases when we found shells in their APCs as well as ammunition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew where it was, when it was, and you've answered that question. Mr. Ivetic, I suggest that you try to resolve the -- the technical issue and that, meanwhile, we proceed. At least we have now a basis -- perhaps for further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to follow up with something you just started talking about. You talked about cases where you found shells in their APCs. Could you tell us, please, what you are talking about, whose APCs, and what did you find.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: We found shells, 81-millimetre mortar shells. That's a standard NATO calibre. We found them in UNPROFOR vehicles, and those vehicles belonged to the French Battalion which was deployed in Butmir airport, in the base there. There was a verbal argument. We did not allow them to proceed because mortar shells of that calibre did not belong to the APC, which meant that they were being taken for the Muslims, who would have then shelled our civilians, our children. And I personally --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can interrupt -- if I can interrupt. Could you explain for us, when you say "mortar shells of that calibre did not belong to the APC," what are you trying to say? What does that mean? Was the APC equipped with mortar -- with a mortar launcher?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. Those APCs were not equipped with mortars. They have infantry weapons, i.e., the APC crews have mortars [as interpreted] and 12.7-millimetre Browning machine-gun rounds. Everything else that was found on an APC was being smuggled to the Muslim side in Sarajevo or outside of Sarajevo for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask clarification, sir. In the transcript at page 81, line 2, you have said that the AP crews had mortars and 12.7-millimetre Browning machine-gun rounds. Is that accurate, sir? Did the APCs have mortars affixed to them the -- the --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. Just the opposite what I said. They did not have mortars and that proves that any mortar rounds found on any APC was being smuggled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Simple question: Did UNPROFOR have any mortars? To your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] UNPROFOR did have mortars, but they were in mortar positions. However, that type of APCs did -- were not equipped with mortars. And when we intervened, we called the corps command, and then the corps command called the battalion command in Butmir, and it turned out that they did it independently and they had to return to the base, which also proves that those rounds were intended for the Muslims and were being smuggled to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us what you observed, what you saw, what you heard, and don't tell us what all that proves. Because it's for the parties to argue what this proves or does not prove, and it's for this Chamber to decide what the evidence proves. So just limit yourself to what you saw, preferably personally saw or heard from others, and don't draw any conclusions, because that confuses the Chamber slightly. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to find out about any other incidents of ammunition or explosives being transported in humanitarian aid or humanitarian equipment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, there were many such cases, and one of them was very typical. Another relative of mine, who was a member of the border police, found things in oxygen containers. This was also recorded by a video camera. We're talking about very large containers that can contain between 100 and 200 kilos of explosive. There was gunpowder and explosives in them, and during the control it was established that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You did not personally observe that, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was my cousin. However, I saw it on TV and I heard it from my cousin personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if there is any documentation recording of that, and it comes to my mind - I've forgotten much from the past - but somewhere in the back of my mind it says that oxygen bottles were recorded and documented. Rather than to hear second-hand from this witness who has not observed it personally, perhaps we could look at that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, our goal is to try to corroborate those documents with hearsay testimony which, I believe, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal does allow and which the Prosecution relied on heavily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I noticed that this witness says that he heard from his brother and saw on television about oxygen bottles, and that already is a corroboration. And I think it was not argued that this is not permissible. Yes. But whether we should hear all the details, but you leave it in your hands. It's your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it's almost over, your time but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More than over, says my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could turn to page 7 of your statement, which is D468, paragraph 28 of the same, in relation to G10 in Hrasnica mentions a Fikret Pljevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like it turn to Exhibit D00156 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could -- perhaps if we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please have P0592 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the same, I could introduce it to tell that you it is dated the 6th of April, 1995, and originates from General Milosevic and is sent to your brigade. It is an order to prepare an aerial bomb and says: "The most profitable target must be selected in Hrasnica or Sokolovic colony where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted." Can you tell me how such an order would be interpreted and implemented by your brigade upon its receipt?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that we were constantly warned by the commander of the VRS and from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that we should adhere to Geneva Conventions, that we had to comply with rules of war, this would exclusively apply to military targets and it did apply to military targets and nothing else. Civilian targets were absolutely excluded from this order. That was the stance of our Main Staff, the corps command, and us in the brigade, in the battalions. All the time civilians had to be protected and excluded from military activities, and this order can only be explained in that way, because that was the only way to achieve the desired effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to be clear, can this order be properly understood or interpreted as ordering the use of bombs against civilian personnel from a military standpoint, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Not at all. The use against civilian population is absolutely excluded, not only in terms of aerial bombs. We were forbidden to open fire on personnel in -- not wearing uniform, let alone civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir, what can you tell me about the casualties suffered by your brigade and by civilians in the Ilidza municipality during the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: In my brigade, we had 460 dead, 2.150 wounded, of whom several hundred seriously wounded. About 400 civilians were -- were killed in Serbian Ilidza, most of them children. This bears witness to the fighting and the kind of fighting the Ilidza Brigade was engaged in. We had four brigades of Muslims, 101st, 102nd, 103rd, and 105th Muslim Brigades on our separation line --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Our final number was 2.000. There were six enemy offensives that were launched against the Serbian Ilidza. Why so many offensives in Serbian Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can interrupt. Could you clarify for us how many enemy offensives were launched against Ilidza by the enemy? The number. How many?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: 36. 36. I don't know if you heard me the first time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One last question for you, sir. Based on your knowledge, how many potential military targets would you have known to have existed on the part of the territory controlled by the ABiH in Sarajevo; and what do you base that assessment on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: About 1.000 military targets existed in Sarajevo and I based that assessment on the following. The commander of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army, which controlled Sarajevo, stated before this Tribunal that they had between 75.000 and 80.000 people under arms --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have to speak slowly for the interpreters to be able to do their job.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 25 brigades with four battalions. That's 100 battalions each. A battalion had four companies. And that means 400 command posts all together, ranging from companies to brigades. If we assume that each of the brigades has a minimum of 20 heavy pieces of artillery, that is 500, plus 400, that's 900, and if we know that during the war Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your explanation. Mr. Ivetic, I'm also looking at the clock. Apparently what the witness tells us is that he deduces the number of potential military targets by analysing the number of troops and the way in which they were organised and then draws his conclusions --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on the basis of that. If that is the explanation, then we have understood it. Even without going into further details, we know the type of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'm happy to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have to adjourn for the day. Do you have any further questions for the witness? You'd announced that as the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, that was the last question. I just have the videotape that hopefully I will figure out and then rest the [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll see that. Witness, Mr. Mijatovic, we adjourn for the day and we will resume on Monday, after the weekend, at 9.30 in the morning. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have already given or testimony still to be given on Monday. There's a fair chance that we would conclude your testimony on Monday. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could -- could Victims and Witness Section explain to the witness over the weekend that greeting of the accused is not something one does as a witness when entering or leaving the courtroom. Then we adjourn for the day, and we will resume, the 26th of May, Monday, the 26th of May, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of May, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.22 p.m.,
